item.title: Press Review — 2026-09-03
item.description:
Across Europe in the past week, most directly documented developments involve political or politically connected figures altering or being pushed to alter their online speech, rather than clear-cut formal censorship by courts or regulators. In France and Malta, both Rima Hassan’s deleted tweet and Teddie Abela’s removed Facebook post illustrate how controversial or embarrassing digital statements can trigger rapid takedowns under political, legal, or social pressure.[1][3] At the regulatory level, Google’s decision to stop applying certain manual demotion measures to EU users demonstrates how European competition and digital rules are reshaping platforms’ control over the visibility of content, including political material.[8] Separately, the ongoing French case of Russian commentator Xenia Fedorova highlights how digital propaganda activities intersect with migration and security decisions, even if not framed explicitly as content moderation.[9] Overall, the picture is one of incremental, sometimes opaque constraints on online political expression, driven as much by strategic self‑censorship and regulatory compliance as by overt state‑ordered takedowns.

item.title: Press Review — 2026-09-02
item.description:
Across Europe in the past week, most reported incidents concern controversial or provocative social media statements by politicians rather than direct government-ordered deletions. French figures such as Rima Hassan and Manon Aubry, German leaders including Sahra Wagenknecht and Alice Weidel, and Finnish and Belgian actors have all drawn criticism or institutional responses for sharp or derogatory online remarks.[1][8][9][10][12][14] Regulatory and systemic issues also feature prominently: Poland is pressing the EU to sanction Meta over scam and deceptive ads, while investigative reporting highlights Kremlin-linked bot networks manipulating discourse around Swedish and French leaders.[4][6][13] Content removal or alteration appears mainly through self-deletion of posts and media corrections after complaints, rather than formal court censorship orders.[1][11] Overall, the picture is of an increasingly contested digital public sphere in Europe, where political speech online triggers party discipline, diplomatic friction, and regulatory pressure but only limited explicit legal suppression in the period observed.

item.title: Press Review — 2026-09-01
item.description:
Across Europe this week, digital speech involving political and public figures continues to provoke legal, diplomatic and regulatory reactions. In France, Rima Hassan’s deleted tweet about a historic militant attack has led to terrorism‑apology investigations and UN interventions, underlining how criminal law is being applied to online political expression.[1][2] EU and national authorities are simultaneously tightening platform obligations under the Digital Services Act and invoking online safety powers, pressing Meta and other large services to redesign systems and remove harmful or addictive content.[3][9][11][14] Civil-society actors and courts are pushing back, with NGOs in the Netherlands alleging censorship of LGBTQ+ accounts and France’s top court striking down a social media ban for under‑15s as disproportionate.[5][13] Diplomatic and media cases—from Belgium’s rebuke of a US ambassador’s mocking post to a UK outlet’s quiet rewriting of an article about Giorgia Meloni—show that both official and editorial speech online remains highly sensitive, with corrections and restraints often occurring after controversy has already emerged.[7][10][15]

item.title: Press Review — 2026-08-31
item.description:
Recent European coverage highlights a dual trend: courts and some policymakers are resisting sweeping restrictions on social media access, while governments and regulators continue to pressure platforms to tighten controls in specific areas. France’s Constitutional Council has repeatedly blocked expansive measures, striking down both an under-15 social media ban and identity-verification requirements on free-expression grounds, even as EU institutions debate softer, more targeted ways to protect minors online.[2][3][6][12] At the same time, the European Commission and other actors are pushing Meta, TikTok and similar platforms to increase content monitoring and adjust “addictive” design features, particularly around migration and youth safety, which can indirectly reshape access to political speech.[5][8][11] Outside the EU, Belarus’s designation of EU-funded information sites as “extremist” and Russia’s broader censorship record underscore continuing efforts by neighbouring regimes to suppress critical digital speech.[4][6][10] Individual politicians, such as Rima Hassan in France, also remain at the centre of controversies over provocative social media posts and subsequent deletions, illustrating how online speech by public figures is closely scrutinised within this evolving regulatory environment.[1]

item.title: Press Review — 2026-08-28
item.description:
Across Europe this week, the central dynamic is a clash between expansive regulatory efforts to control social media and strong legal and civil-liberties resistance, most visibly in France where the Constitutional Council has struck down a youth social media ban on freedom-of-expression and privacy grounds.[1][2][3][8][15] EU institutions and several member states continue to push for tighter controls, including possible access bans for minors, design changes to reduce addictive features, rapid takedown powers for criminal recruitment content, and enforcement of safety and fraud standards against major platforms.[5][7][11][12][13] Governments such as the UK and Sweden are invoking new laws to demand removal of harmful or criminal content, while platforms like Meta face pressure and potential fines over perceived moderation failures.[9][11][12] At the same time, Telegram’s Pavel Durov alleges secret political demands for censorship and surveillance, underscoring tensions between state security or political interests and platform commitments to privacy and speech.[6][14] Overall, the European landscape shows intensifying regulatory and enforcement activity around digital public speech, tempered by constitutional and rights-based constraints that are beginning to define boundaries for state control of online expression.[1][3][8][10][15]

item.title: Press Review — 2026-08-27
item.description:
Recent European coverage highlights a growing clash between efforts to regulate harmful or sensitive online content and legal protections for freedom of expression. France’s Constitutional Council significantly curtailed a strict social media access and identity-verification law, while EU-level initiatives and national politicians continue pressing platforms like TikTok and Meta for tougher content controls and design changes.[2][3][5][11][13] At the same time, cases such as Belarus branding EU-funded sites “extremist” and European telecom operators seeking blocking powers over child abuse material show how legal tools can be used both to suppress politically linked content and to target clearly illegal material.[9][15] Informal pressure is also in focus, with Telegram’s founder alleging governmental demands for censorship and surveillance, and corporate filtering decisions—as in Heinz’s labelling policy—becoming flashpoints when amplified by political actors.[6][10] Overall, the landscape is one of expanding regulatory and political scrutiny of digital speech, with courts occasionally pushing back and ongoing debates about how far content removal and blocking powers should extend.

item.title: Press Review — 2026-08-18
item.description:
